This episode differs fundamentally because macroprudential policy has shifted from theoretical design and baseline calibration to active post-pandemic vulnerability management, where systemic risk monitoring explicitly targets the buildup of leverage in non-bank financial intermediation and commercial real estate. Unlike the mid-2010s—when the tool was brand new and regulators were overly cautious about signaling distress—current Fed leadership views a positive CCyB not as an emergency brake, but as a standard structural feature for building baseline resilience.

no_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the post-2016 implementation era when the CCyB was established at 0% and maintained there, and the March 2020 pandemic shock when the Fed actively cut the buffer to 0% to free up lending capacity rather than raising it. It differs from the 2020 episode because the Fed has consistently maintained the buffer at 0% through various post-pandemic growth cycles, showing a deep institutional reluctance to activate a tool that has never once been deployed in a tightening direction during non-crisis expansions. The Fed treats 0% as the default operational steady-state rather than a floor to be lifted proactively, distinguishing this period from jurisdictions like the UK or Switzerland that routinely cycle their buffers.
